newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer muddies German rate speculation waters.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer muddies German rate speculation waters.

text.p: The monetary leanings of Germany's powerful Bundesbank grew ever more unclear on Friday as Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he saw no need for easier interest rate policy in the foreseeable future.

The comment followed on the heels remarks from a pair of his fellow council members which seemed to suggest that a rate cut was indeed possible in this business cycle -- comments which had sent German stocks and European bonds higher.

Tietmeyer, in an interview with German radio to be broadcast on Sunday, said that he saw 1996 economic growth of one percent or more and that interest rates were not now standing in the way of economic growth.
"And I am assuming that there is a strong chance that (such growth) will continue into next year," he said.
The comments were the latest twist in a string of remarks from the Bundesbank that have sent conflicting signals about the central bank's intentions regarding interest rates.

Speaking at separate events earlier on Friday, Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing and council member Ernst Welteke stressed there was no need to cut rates now, but held out hope that the central bank could consider a further easing.

Issing, whose comments in a German television interview last Wednesday nixed financial market hopes for lower rates, was asked in Brussels if he meant to rule out any rate cuts forever. He responded, "Of course not. There is never an end."
Meanwhile, Welteke told reporters in Frankfurt that in the medium term, "a repo cut is still possible depending on developments."
The remarks provoked a sharp jump in German bonds and stocks, and elsewhere in Europe as speculation spread that the central bank may still be ready to lower yields and fan economic growth.
"The market is incredibly nervous right now," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS. "A segment of the market saw these comments and decided it had to jump on the bandwagon."
Only two days ago, Issing quashed rate cut hopes, saying "key rates are at a historic low here and nothing more is to be expected or necessary."

That remark, combined with the Bundesbank's decision to keep rates on hold at its regular council meeting on Thursday, led many to believe that with the economy here on the mend, the central bank had decided not to lower rates any further in the current business cycle.
The discount rate already stands at a historic low level of 2.5 percent, the emergency Lombard lending facility at 4.5 percent, and the securities repurchase rate at 3.00 percent.
Some analysts said Friday's comments were a deliberate move to soften Issing's strong words on Wednesday.

Indeed Welteke, unusually speaking for another member of the Bundesbank council, said he did not think that Issing intended "with his little comment to take interest rate speculation out of the market for all time".
Harry Thapar, analyst at MCM YieldWatch in London, said that remark showed the Bundesbank was trying to at least leave the door open to further rate cuts.
"Issing's tone on Wednesday was very aggressive, they wanted to calm things," he said.
Others, however, said today's remarks were only stating the obvious and that nervous financial markets, eager to jump on latest headline, were overstating Bundesbank intentions.
"Issing has said the same thing several times in recent weeks," Fahrinkrug said. "The market has lost its orientation and in these situations, the smallest comments will move it."
